title: Video: Towards An Uncertain Winter For Energy
gist: Five months into the US-Iran war, Strait of Hormuz transit has collapsed from 17-20mn bpd of oil to under 1mn bpd and roughly a quarter of global LNG trade is off the market, swinging the oil balance from surplus into a 7-8mn bpd deficit and doubling Asian and European gas benchmarks. With EU gas stores below 60% full and at the bottom of their five-year range, Europe faces a bidding war with Asia for US and Russian LNG cargoes, and a cold winter would force a repeat of the 2022 playbook of subsidies plus industrial demand destruction.

themes.theme: Escalation dynamics and why diplomacy keeps failing

insights.claim: Peace talks between the US and Iran keep collapsing because intermediaries negotiate with the Iranian foreign ministry and parliament while the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps actually controls the fighting, and the IRGC launches fresh attacks whenever diplomatic progress appears.
insights.speaker: Tom Holland
insights.so_what: Treat headline ceasefire or MoU news as a fade rather than a trade: durable de-escalation requires IRGC buy-in, so energy risk premia should not be sold on foreign-ministry statements alone.
insights.quote: every time that we see some diplomatic progress, the Revolutionary Guards appear to launch new attacks, whether on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz or on US allies around the region, that then sees the diplomatic efforts break down
insights.locator: And part of the problem there is

insights.claim: Despite a US-Iran memorandum of understanding on peace signed six weeks earlier, Iran launched ballistic missiles at a US airbase in Jordan over a recent weekend and the US retaliated, so active fighting has resumed.
insights.speaker: Tom Holland
insights.so_what: A signed peace document has already failed once; positioning should assume the conflict persists into the Northern Hemisphere winter rather than pricing a near-term resolution.
insights.quote: There were some hopes for a renewed ceasefire over the weekend. Iran then launched ballistic missiles at a US airbase in Jordan. The US has retaliated.
insights.locator: Well, diplomacy does continue

insights.claim: The conflict is widening geographically, with Saudi Arabia attacking Iranian proxies in Iraq and a drone strike hitting a floating re-gasification facility near Port Said in Egypt.
insights.speaker: Tom Holland
insights.so_what: Energy infrastructure outside the Gulf, including regas terminals in the Mediterranean and Red Sea corridor, is now a target set; insurance, shipping and infrastructure risk should be repriced beyond Hormuz.
insights.quote: we've just seen a drone attack on a re-gasification plant, a floating re-gasification facility near Portside in Egypt
insights.locator: And possibly even more concerning

insights.claim: Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains largely suspended, with only sporadic traffic amounting to a tanker here and an LNG carrier there.
insights.speaker: Tom Holland
insights.so_what: Hormuz transit counts are the single highest-frequency indicator to monitor; a sustained return of convoy traffic would be the first hard signal to unwind long energy exposure.
insights.locator: So the upshot is that

themes.theme: Oil supply shock and the limits of bypass routes

insights.claim: Oil and petroleum product flows through the Strait of Hormuz have collapsed from a pre-war 17-20mn barrels a day to just a few hundred thousand to one million barrels a day.
insights.speaker: Tom Holland
insights.so_what: This is the largest physical crude supply interruption available to model; anchor oil price scenarios to the size of this gap rather than to headline geopolitical risk premia.
insights.quote: somewhere between 17 million barrels a day and 20 million barrels a day of oil and petroleum products transited through the Strait of Hormuz. Now, that has fallen to, well, really just a few hundred thousand or a million barrels a day
insights.locator: Well, if we look back before the beginning of this war

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia has raised loadings at its Red Sea terminal of Yanbu to around 5mn barrels a day from about 1mn barrels a day before the conflict, and the UAE is pushing as much crude as it can to Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman.
insights.speaker: Tom Holland
insights.so_what: Bypass pipeline capacity is already close to maxed out at roughly 4mn bpd of incremental Saudi relief, so further escalation has little remaining physical buffer to absorb it.
insights.quote: Saudi Arabia has been loading around 5 million barrels a day at its Red Sea terminal of Yenbo, up from around 1 million barrels a day before the conflict
insights.locator: Now, countries in the region have tried to compensate

insights.claim: Even after bypass routes are accounted for, the Gulf shipping interruption has removed roughly 10-11mn barrels a day from global oil supply.
insights.speaker: Tom Holland
insights.so_what: A net 10-11mn bpd loss dwarfs OPEC spare capacity and strategic reserve release capability, implying prices clear through demand destruction rather than supply response.
insights.quote: we have seen really a deficit of around about 10 to 11 million barrels a day in global supply caused by the interruption of shipping through the Gulf
insights.locator: But even with these attempts to bypass

insights.claim: The global oil market was in surplus before the war, but the disruption has more than absorbed that cushion and pushed the balance into a deficit of 7-8mn barrels a day, which is driving prices higher.
insights.speaker: Tom Holland
insights.so_what: Pre-war bearish surplus arguments are void; the market is structurally short until either Hormuz reopens or 7-8mn bpd of demand is destroyed.
insights.quote: we've seen a big reduction of 7 or 8 million barrels a day into deficit as a result of this conflict
insights.locator: Now, yes, the global market had been in surplus

themes.theme: LNG dislocation: Qatar offline, US cannot fill the hole

insights.claim: About a quarter of the world's liquefied natural gas trade transited the Strait of Hormuz before the conflict, most of it Qatari, and that flow has essentially ground to a halt.
insights.speaker: Tom Holland
insights.so_what: A quarter of seaborne gas supply vanishing sets a floor under global gas benchmarks and favours US and other non-Gulf LNG exporters with uncontracted volumes.
insights.quote: we saw something like a quarter of the world's trade in liquefied natural gas transiting through the Strait of Hormuz, most of that originating in Qatar
insights.locator: That's right. Before the conflict

insights.claim: US LNG exports have risen from around 15 billion cubic feet a day in 2025 to roughly 18 bcf/d, a faster ramp than anyone expected given that new export terminal rollout times are inflexible.
insights.speaker: Tom Holland
insights.so_what: US export infrastructure is running above consensus assumptions, a direct volume tailwind for US liquefaction operators and Henry Hub demand, but it is already near its physical ceiling.
insights.quote: the U.S. exported around 15 billion cubic feet a day of LNG. That's now up to around 18 billion cubic feet a day. That's a really bigger increase than anyone expected
insights.locator: Now, again, we have seen other producers attempt to compensate

insights.claim: The 3 bcf/d increase in US LNG exports cannot offset the roughly 10 bcf/d of Qatari supply lost, leaving a structural gas shortfall of around 7 bcf/d.
insights.speaker: Tom Holland
insights.so_what: The arithmetic makes elevated gas prices a supply-side certainty rather than a sentiment trade; the shortfall can only close via weather, demand destruction or Hormuz reopening.
insights.quote: A 3 billion cubic feet a day increase from the U.S. can't compensate for what amounts almost to 10 billion cubic feet a day lost from Qatari's supply.
insights.locator: But that can't compensate for the reduction

insights.claim: The Asian JKM LNG benchmark is trading at the equivalent of roughly $120 a barrel of oil, having doubled since the outbreak of the conflict.
insights.speaker: Tom Holland
insights.so_what: Gas is now pricing at a premium to crude on an energy-equivalent basis, incentivising gas-to-oil switching in Asian power and industry and supporting fuel oil and diesel demand.
insights.quote: the JKM benchmark in Asia for liquefied natural gas, that's now trading at the equivalent of about $120 a barrel for oil. That's doubled since the outbreak of the conflict.
insights.locator: So, again, we have seen prices rise

insights.claim: Europe's TTF gas benchmark in the Netherlands is trading around EUR60 per megawatt hour, equivalent to roughly $110 a barrel of oil, more than double its pre-conflict level.
insights.speaker: Tom Holland
insights.so_what: EUR60/MWh is the marked level to track; European industrial margins, utility hedging and inflation prints all key off moves above this into winter.
insights.quote: if we look at Europe and the TTF benchmark in the Netherlands, it is now trading at around 60 euros per megawatt hour. That's the equivalent of about $110 a barrel for oil.
insights.locator: Similarly, if we look at Europe

insights.claim: The JKM-versus-TTF gap, with Asia at roughly $120/bbl-equivalent against Europe at $110/bbl-equivalent, shows Asia is currently outbidding Europe for marginal cargoes.
insights.speaker: Tom Holland
insights.so_what: Watch the JKM-TTF spread as the live gauge of where flexible US cargoes will be diverted; Europe must close the gap to attract enough gas to restock before winter.
insights.locator: So we are seeing stresses in the LNG market

themes.theme: Europe's storage vulnerability and the cargo bidding war

insights.claim: European gas stores are less than 60% full and sit at the very bottom of their five-year range for this time of year, despite summer being the normal period for building winter buffer stocks.
insights.speaker: Tom Holland
insights.so_what: Low entry inventories mean less margin for weather error; European gas is asymmetrically exposed to a cold snap and storage percentage full is the key weekly datapoint.
insights.quote: if we look at European gas stocks now, they're less than 60 percent full. And the European gas stocks are at their lowest level for this time of year for the last five years.
insights.locator: If we look at Europe's gas stores

insights.claim: Europe's direct exposure to the Gulf is small, importing only around 1 bcf/d of Qatari LNG in normal times against Qatar's roughly 10 bcf/d of exports that mostly go to Asia, yet Europe is still badly hit.
insights.speaker: Tom Holland
insights.so_what: Direct import exposure is a misleading risk metric for a fungible seaborne commodity; the transmission runs through competitive bidding for cargoes, not through severed bilateral flows.
insights.quote: normally, Europe doesn't actually buy that much gas from the Persian Gulf. It buys around about, in normal times, a billion cubic feet of equivalent of Qatari LNG each day
insights.locator: In particular, we'll see European buyers competing

insights.claim: Because Qatari volumes are gone, Asian buyers are now competing directly with European buyers for cargoes of US natural gas and of Russian LNG, which will keep prices elevated into the European winter.
insights.speaker: Tom Holland
insights.so_what: Expect sustained upward pressure on European gas through the winter; Russian LNG becomes a contested marginal barrel with obvious sanctions and political complications.
insights.quote: we do see Asia competing with European buyers for cargoes of US natural gas and, indeed, for cargoes of Russian LNG. And this increased competition basically is going to keep prices elevated going into the European winter.
insights.locator: However, because we've seen this overall reduction

insights.claim: Europe entered this shock already cut off from Russian pipeline gas since the Ukraine conflict, leaving it structurally more dependent on the seaborne LNG market now being squeezed.
insights.speaker: Tom Holland
insights.so_what: Europe has no pipeline fallback this time, so the adjustment must come entirely through price and demand rationing rather than substitution.
insights.locator: Okay. So macroeconomically, in terms of that supply condition

themes.theme: The European policy playbook and its self-defeating macro cost

insights.claim: Europe has an established crisis playbook from the Russian invasion of Ukraine: governments step in with fiscal transfers, price caps and subsidies to shield households, alongside reduced gas use by energy-intensive industry.
insights.speaker: Tom Holland
insights.so_what: Anticipate a rerun of 2022-style emergency fiscal packages if winter turns cold, with implications for European sovereign issuance and deficit forecasts.
insights.quote: We saw this European playbook whereby governments stepped in with fiscal measures to mitigate the impact on households with price gaps, with subsidies.
insights.locator: Now, Europe does have a playbook to deal with this

insights.claim: Household energy subsidies and price caps blunt the price signal so households do not cut consumption, which forces the entire burden of demand reduction onto industry and damages output.
insights.speaker: Tom Holland
insights.so_what: The policy response itself is the bear case for European industrials: energy-intensive manufacturers absorb the rationing, so short industrial output and margin exposure rather than consumer names.
insights.quote: if you do have price caps, that, in effect, does not discourage households from using energy. So it doesn't help to reduce energy consumption. And the burden of reduced consumption falls on industry
insights.locator: The problem is, of course

insights.claim: The combination of subsidised households and rationed industry produces a twin hit of rising fiscal stress and weaker growth for Europe.
insights.speaker: Tom Holland
insights.so_what: Position for a European stagflationary impulse into 2026-27 winter: wider deficits and bond supply on one side, downgraded industrial growth on the other.
insights.quote: that increases both fiscal stresses on one hand and weighs on growth on the other hand
insights.locator: So, essentially, if you're in Europe at the moment

insights.claim: With supply constrained, storage depleted and policy tools blunt, the decisive variable for Europe's winter economic outcome is simply the weather.
insights.speaker: Tom Holland
insights.so_what: Treat Northern Hemisphere winter temperature forecasts as a first-order macro input for European assets this season, not a seasonal curiosity.
insights.quote: essentially, if you're in Europe at the moment, you are hoping for a mild winter
insights.locator: So, essentially, if you're in Europe at the moment
